title: Gateless Barrier, Case 22: Mahakasyapa's Flagpole
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk highlights the importance of diligent practice and devotion in spiritual growth, as exemplified by Ananda's story about receiving a transmission from his teacher Mahakasyapa. Nomon Tim Burnett encourages listeners to cultivate a sense of openness and receptivity, allowing them to settle into their true nature and connection with the world. By embracing life's twists and turns and learning to listen deeply, we can tap into the wisdom and guidance that lies within our experiences.

sentences.text: Good evening everybody.
Welcome back to Rishinsama.

You may think I'm a little obsessive telling all the stories in this koan collection, but I was just remembering it's actually a very traditional thing to do, especially in the schools that really study koans as meditation objects.
That's pretty much all the talks are, ever.
So anyway, I just wanted you to know this is legit.
In a way it makes it easier to prepare the talks.
I know what I'm going to talk about.
I know the topic, I guess, but in other ways it makes it much harder, because what are you going to say?
Anyway, the 21st case of the Mumon koan is about deeply responding to whatever it is that's calling, sometimes called the inmost request.
What is life really calling for from you?
Or, it's interesting the way that word calling gets turned around, too: what is your calling?
So here's the story.

Did he give you anything else?"
Mahakasyapa called out, "Ananda."
"Yes," answered Ananda.
"Knock down the flagpole at the gate," said Mahakasyapa.*

They didn't have anything else, so they could really focus on what they heard.
But even by the standard of the time, Ananda had a very good memory, and he was almost always by the Buddha's side when the Buddha would give talks, and Ananda memorized every single one.
If you read the early teachings, they always start with a stock phrase: "Thus have I heard."
You're supposed to be hearing it in Ananda's voice; he's recalling, telling you what he heard.
Later sutras, where they wanted to make sure it sounded legit, started with that whether Ananda was around or not.

Even if Ananda wasn't by the Buddha's side, it would be high pressure on the other monks, because they would know that Ananda would come along a little while later and say, "Well, what did the Buddha say?"
And he would not settle for a summary.
You had to really tell him.
So they all were on their toes, listening very carefully to these teachings.

What I've always appreciated about Ananda is not that he could do that, which is amazing, but that he was so diligent and devoted in his practice, and that he kept going even though in some fundamental way he just didn't get it.
He knew all this stuff and he could recite it.
It's a little more like book knowledge, but he somehow didn't feel like he quite understood the meaning.
What's the true meaning of this?
He didn't quite understand.
Or you could say, if you use the language of awakening, he wasn't awakened.
He wasn't fully enlightened or awake.
He was really close for a long, long time.

I always forget how many.
A hundred and something.
Not that many, really, to go back 2,600 years.
So in the Zen story, Nanda is in this story receiving something from his teacher.

These are all good stories, though, that we should know and appreciate.
In the early Buddhist story, after the Buddha died he did not have one particular disciple.
He had a whole little group of them.
There are different lists of the great disciples, but about a dozen.
After he died, because there was no one teacher, it created a challenge.
The disciples had to figure out: what are we doing?
What's next?
They wanted to clarify what all the teachings were, because they didn't have the Buddha to ask anymore.
So just like us, just like we would do, they said, "Let's have a meeting."
They had a big meeting, later called the First Buddhist Council.
And they had a problem with their meeting.
They realized that the only people who should be at this meeting, to deeply understand and compare notes about the true meaning of Buddhist teachings, are the ones who are awake, who really get it.
Who are fully arhats, is the term they used.

So it all worked out.
But in the Zen story, we have this lovely idea of one teacher transmitting to one student, or transmitting to more than one student.
In the end, there are important lines of transmission, series of ancestors and disciples.
Even if that doesn't always exactly meet historical truth, it is also true.
It is also a very true teaching, I think.
There's something that happens when you practice with somebody for decades.
You study together, as we're trying to do here in our little way.

Something that I was somehow able to at least partially receive.

The main symbol is the robe.
And then usually the bowls, too.

And it's also just fabric.
It came from the fabric store.

But it's also just a thing.

But he knows that's just a robe.
What's the essence?
What else was there?
And his teacher looks at him, and instead of trying to explain anything, calls to him.
Just offers him a small, strong call, calling him by name.
This story also appears in another collection of stories by Keizan Zenji, stories of each of these transmissions from Buddha to his teacher.
I saw this story in there, and something about it really struck me.
This "yes": what was this yes about?
What is it to be called and really say yes?
I sat with this question for a while, a year or two or something.
At one point I was talking to Norman about it a lot.
He was probably getting tired of hearing about it.
And then one time at Samish, this thing about the flagpole somehow came to me.
So let me give you the back story on the flagpole.
The last line, after he has called and says yes, the teacher Mahakasyapa says, "Knock down the flagpole at the gate."

You could go watch.

You memorize those.
But anyway, if you won the debate, they'd put up your flag or something like that.

It's not winning or losing.
It's "knock down the flagpole."
You don't need the flagpole anymore.
There's no putting your flag up and down.
You don't need that.
Knock it down.

Stop trying to run your flag up there.
Knock it down.
So anyway, I was at Samish, at sesshin.
You know how in the wind, if there's no flag on the flagpole, it makes this kind of ding, ding, ding, ding, weird sound?
It's a little bit annoying and you barely notice it.
I don't think there's actually a flagpole at Samish, but for some reason I was hearing this sound.

What is the flagpole?
What is it?

And he says, [unclear: "I remember this really clearly.

This is often some kind of meditation posture, whatever feels right right now.

So try that.
Let's try that for a couple of minutes.

Just exhaling, yes.
Just giving yourself over to this yes.
Trying that.
How's it feeling, huh?

Calling deeply to yourself.

Isn't that great?
Settling the self on the self and letting your life flower bloom.
Yes!

Let's appreciate that again.
You've probably heard this many times, but it's always worth considering some great works like this.
So here's "Wild Geese" by Mary Oliver.
Let's just focus on this sense of the world, the geese calling us.
*You do not have to be good.
You do not have to walk on your knees for a hundred miles through the desert repenting.
You only have to let the soft animal of your body love what it loves.
Tell me about despair.
Yours.
And I will tell you mine.
Meanwhile the world goes on.
Meanwhile the sun and the clear pebbles of the rain are moving across the landscapes, over the prairies and the deep trees, the mountains and the rivers.
Meanwhile the wild geese, high in the clean blue air, are heading home again.
Whoever you are, no matter how lonely, the world offers itself to your imagination, calls to you like the wild geese, harsh and exciting, over and over announcing your place in the family of things.*
*The world offers itself to your imagination, calls to you like the wild geese, harsh and exciting, over and over announcing your place in the family of things.
The world offering itself to you, calling to you, harsh and exciting, over and over, patiently calling to you.*
I think the poem and the case remind us, though, that the calling itself is not enough.
It is not complete.
The world's calls, or your life calling to you, could just be landing on deaf ears.
Or maybe you're halfway hearing it but don't quite listen.
Don't quite believe it, don't quite agree: "Oh, I don't agree with that."
So the calls of the world by themselves are not enough.
We need to show up.
We need to actually really listen.
We need to find out how to say yes.
I was thinking about this with a group earlier today.
I asked them, and I could ask you too, I guess: just think for a moment how your life ended up.
Would you have predicted this?
Probably not.
Maybe some little details, but the whole thing?
You never could have predicted this.
So somehow life called to you and you've been trying to answer all this time.
Disasters and problems and losses called to you.
Joy and love called to you.
Your many brilliant ideas called to you.
Some of them turned out not to be too brilliant after all.
Somehow we are trying to answer.
Our whole life is nothing but like Ananda.
Trying to answer: what is this?
How do I say yes to this?
And we don't quite pull it off.
We know about that.
And yet even in the suffering, there is some truth.
There is some feeling.
There is something we are receiving, warm hand to warm hand, from all of our teachers.
Sometimes we don't recognize our teachers, but they are always teaching us.
So how has that been for you?
What have you learned, trying to answer the calls of the world?
When your teacher calls your name.
Let's think about that.
Let that be part of our conversation.
*Tensions equally extend to every*
